weaknesses: The tests outlined in Section 7 are missing the specific decision each test is meant to inform, making them less actionable.
The brief introduces an unexplained 'evidence-weighted count' metric throughout, which causes confusion and clutters the data.

While it correctly flags templated responses for setup effort, it misses that the willingness-to-pay answers (P01, P04, P10) and recipe time requirements (P01, P04) are also identically templated, treating them as independent verification.
The brief fails to explicitly state the overall limits of the research evidence, such as the small qualitative sample size.

traps.excerpt: P06 was excluded from all customer findings due to severe interviewer bias and leading questions
Identical templated concerns emerged across interviews: P02, P05, P07, P08, and P10 each warned: "Setup has to be fast. If I need to type in my whole pantry I'll quit on day two."
Out-of-target: Single student living alone (P07; raw count 1, evidence-weighted count 0.25).
The assumption that all multi-person households who cook weeknights need dinner planning is unvalidated, as shown by retired couple P09 who cook daily without friction
An outlier was P08, who stated an intent to pay thirty euros a month, but this was anchored entirely to a single holiday spoilage incident rather than routine meal planning
Riskiest assumption: Households will keep a pantry and fridge inventory up to date in an app
A rigid weekly dinner plan may not match household cooking realities [P05:t1, P05:t4, P08:t1]. P05 previously abandoned a meal planning app because an unfollowed plan felt like failure

The claim that the app will stop household arguments is weakly supported, being reported as dinner friction by only 1 couple (P02), and is better reframed as a shared list and purchasing coordination problem
The market contains established tools addressing either inventory tracking or weekly meal planning, contradicting the idea brief claim that existing recipe apps do not know what you own

PlanPlate (EUR 2.99/month, last verified 2024-11-05) offers meal planning calendars, though its data may be outdated [C:PlanPlate]. ZeroWaste Kitchen (Free/donations, last verified 2025-01-20) offers leftover recipes, though its data may also be outdated [C:ZeroWaste Kitchen]. WeekWise offers budget plans for a EUR 29.99 one-off fee (verified 2026-05-02), but its details are unsourced in the market registry

Market snippet S06 claiming 25% annual market growth is unsupported due to missing source and date [S06]. Market snippet S07 claiming 73% of families struggle with dinner decisions is unsupported due to missing source and date [S07]. Market snippet S08 claiming 97% of households would pay for automated meal planning comes from an unreliable blog source and is unsupported [S08]. Market snippet S09 citing 4% online grocery share is stale data from 2016

criteria.justification: The brief covers all six required areas comprehensively and with significant detail and substance.
Claims are thoroughly cited and mostly well-grounded, though it misses that some answers (willingness-to-pay and recipe time) were templated, and the 'evidence-weighted count' is confusing.
The brief correctly weighs the evidence, expertly discounts bad data (like P06 and S06-S09), explicitly notes contradictory statements, and properly frames WTP outliers.
The recommendation is clear and tests include who, what, how many, and a success metric, but they completely omit the decision each test informs.
The brief is well-structured and concise, but the repetitive inclusion of raw counts alongside an unexplained 'evidence-weighted count' creates slight reading friction.
